source.title: Game exposure shapes intensity and performance in Division I college football

paper.citation: Lever, J. R., Fusco, A., Landow, L., Hunt, R., Leiszler, M., Appelman, A., Ramaeker, J., & Wagle, J. P. (2026). Game exposure shapes intensity and performance in Division I college football. Journal of Sports Sciences, 1–12. https://doi.org/10.1080/02640414.2026.2705698
paper.abstract: Across Division I football games, how do snap exposure and position relate to total and per-snap external training load, and how are those load metrics associated with offensive and defensive PFF grades? Longitudinal observational data comprised 4,084 player-games from 232 athletes, 88 games, and 10 seasons within one NCAA Division I football program. Players were grouped as Bigs, Mids, Skills, or quarterbacks and by game exposure: low (0–22 snaps), moderate (23–49), or high (≥50). Offensive, defensive, and special-teams series coded as active participation were retained; the program, competitive level, and athlete sex are not described in enough detail to infer transfer beyond this setting. Catapult Vector S wearables quantified PlayerLoad, total and relative-speed distance, accelerations, decelerations, and impacts during active game participation; quality control screened signal loss, implausible values, and device malfunction. Snap counts and PFF grades were linked to wearable data. Every snap was treated as an equivalent exposure unit despite differences in duration, rest, and tactical demand. Linear mixed models included athlete and game random intercepts, snap category and position fixed effects, Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons, and separate offensive and defensive grade models for each load metric.
paper.tldr: This study directly informs collegiate American-football workload interpretation by separating cumulative game load from per-snap intensity and examining how both vary with playing exposure, position, and PFF performance grades. Total external load increased across exposure groups, but per-snap load decreased. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Catapult Vector S wearables quantified PlayerLoad, total and relative-speed distance, accelerations, decelerations, and impacts during active game participation; quality control screened signal loss, implausible values, and device malfunction. Snap counts and PFF grades were linked to wearable data. Every snap was treated as an equivalent exposure unit despite differences in duration, rest, and tactical demand. Linear mixed models included athlete and game random intercepts, snap category and position fixed effects, Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons, and separate offensive and defensive grade models for each load metric.
paper.findings: Total external load increased across exposure groups, but per-snap load decreased. Per-snap PlayerLoad was 8.73 AU·snap−1 lower for moderate versus low exposure (95% CI 7.71–9.76; d=0.83) and 11.60 AU·snap−1 lower for high versus low exposure (95% CI 10.50–12.70; d=1.10). Exposure-related reductions in per-snap load occurred across positional groups, although absolute and per-snap loads varied by position and metric. On offense, total PlayerLoad (β=0.015, p<0.001), sprinting distance (β=0.0108, p=0.001), and impact count (β=0.106, p<0.001) were positively associated with PFF grade. On defense, total-load associations were limited, while higher per-snap running, sprinting, acceleration, and deceleration metrics were associated with lower PFF grades (all p<0.01). These load–grade relationships are phase-specific associations and do not demonstrate that accumulating load improves offense or that higher intensity causes worse defense.
paper.limitations: A single Division I program across changing seasons, schemes, coaches, player roles, injuries, and technology limits external validity. PFF grades are analyst-derived, role- and opportunity-dependent proxies rather than independently validated objective outcomes; small grade differences should not be treated as definitive performance changes. Snap count ignores play duration, between-play recovery, tempo, score, weather, opponent quality, and tactical assignment. Hardware or firmware changes over a decade and inclusion of special-teams snaps may distort exposure-normalized comparisons, particularly among low-exposure players. Performance analyses modeled several load metrics separately; the findings are exploratory and vulnerable to residual confounding and multiplicity. Low per-snap output among high-exposure players may reflect pacing, role, play context, survivor/selection effects, or measurement structure rather than fatigue alone.
paper.practicalImplications: Report cumulative game load and per-snap intensity together and annotate role, phase, special teams, and game context. Do not classify a high-load offensive performance as inherently good or a high-intensity defensive performance as inefficient without film and assignment review. Use exposure groups to describe demands and prepare role transitions, but establish team-specific distributions before setting training or recovery thresholds. The study supports contextual workload review in collegiate American football, not causal prescriptions or universal cut points.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. paper.rtp: This study did not directly evaluate rehabilitation or return to sport. It provides no standalone clearance criterion, reinjury threshold, or validated return-to-play progression.
